common_name: Sweetie Pie Pepper (AAS-Winning Miniature Bell Pepper for Kids and Containers)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights stay reliably above 55 degrees F; Sweetie Pie is a 2017 All-America Selections winner bred as a true miniature bell pepper small enough for little hands and container gardens.

directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all danger of frost has passed, and stake the heavily-laden plants to keep fruit off the ground. Sweetie Pie produces abundant 2.5-3 inch, thick-walled miniature bell peppers that can be picked green or left to sweeten to red, on compact plants that excel in hot, humid conditions where standard bells often struggle. Its small fruit size and sweet flavor make it a favorite for introducing children to growing and eating vegetables. Harvest regularly to keep plants productive through the full warm season.

common_name: Hot Sunset Pepper (AAS-Winning Early Hot Wax Pepper)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Hot Sunset, a 2015 All-America Selections winner, is a hot wax-type pepper bred for an earlier, more prolific harvest than older wax pepper varieties.

directions: Transplant into full sun after the last frost in well-fertilized soil, feeding regularly to support heavy, early fruit set. Hot Sunset ripens elongated, tapered banana-shaped pods from green to red, carrying a moderate heat that works well fresh, grilled, roasted, or pickled. The variety also offers resistance to Xanthomonas bacterial spot and tomato spotted wilt virus, improving reliability where those diseases are common. No staking is required, though sturdy support helps under especially heavy fruit loads.

common_name: Giant Ristra Pepper (AAS-Winning Large Chile for Drying and Stringing)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Giant Ristra, a 2014 All-America Selections winner, carries cayenne-level heat on a Marconi-shaped fruit and is bred specifically for stringing into traditional drying ristras.

directions: Transplant into full sun in well-drained soil after the last frost, spacing plants closely since the bushy habit needs little room and rarely requires staking. Giant Ristra bears heavy yields of bright red, 6-7 inch elongated horn-shaped chiles carrying cayenne-level heat, with a flavor suited to fresh use, roasting, or drying. The thin-walled pods dry quickly once strung into ristras, making this variety a strong choice for gardeners who want a traditional dried red chile harvest. Reduce watering as fruit matures to concentrate flavor and speed drying.
sources: New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute

common_name: Pole Seychelles Bean (AAS-Winning Dutch Stringless Pole Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed once soil has warmed; Pole Seychelles is a 2017 All-America Selections winner from Dutch breeders Bakker Brothers, grown on a 5-6 foot trellis for repeated harvests through the season.

directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep at the base of a sturdy 5-6 foot trellis or support in full sun, since this is a true climbing pole type. Pole Seychelles produces long, slender, uniform, stringless 5-6 inch pods with excellent flavor on vigorous dark-green vines, yielding multiple flushes of pods across the growing season rather than one concentrated harvest. The variety carries resistance to Bean Common Mosaic Virus, improving reliability in humid climates. Trim vine growth once it reaches the top of the trellis to encourage fuller pod set lower on the plant, and pick every few days to keep production going.

common_name: Parisian Gherkin Cucumber (AAS-Winning Mini Pickling Cucumber)

planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed to at least 70 degrees F after the last frost; Parisian Gherkin, a 2015 All-America Selections winner, is a semi-vining mini cucumber bred specifically for midget pickles.

directions: Direct sow into warm, fertile soil in full sun, or grow in a large patio container, since the semi-vining habit stays compact. Parisian Gherkin produces numerous small, black-spined cucumbers best harvested at the midget or small-pickle stage for crisp, sweet flavor, though it can also be enjoyed fresh in salads. The variety carries resistance to scab and cucumber mosaic virus with tolerance to powdery mildew, giving it good vigor through a long picking season. Water deeply and infrequently rather than with frequent light sprinklings to encourage strong root development and reduce disease pressure.
sources: university extension AAS trial garden reports

common_name: Mountain Rouge Tomato (AAS-Winning Disease-Resistant Pink Beefsteak)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights are reliably mild; Mountain Rouge, a 2019 All-America Selections winner, is an indeterminate pink beefsteak bred to perform especially well in cooler climates.

directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, then transplant into full sun with sturdy caging or staking for the vigorous indeterminate vines. Mountain Rouge yields large, 12-14 ounce pink beefsteak fruits with a balanced sweet-acid heirloom-style flavor and minimal seed, and it carries resistance to Late Blight, Verticillium wilt, Fusarium wilt, and root-knot nematode for improved reliability. It performs notably well in cooler growing regions where many beefsteak types struggle to size up fully. Feed and water consistently through fruit set to support the large fruit size.

common_name: Winter Honeybaby Squash (AAS-Winning Compact Personal-Size Butternut-Type)

planting.note: Direct sow (or transplant) after the last frost once soil has warmed to at least 65 degrees F; Winter Honeybaby, a 2017 All-America Selections winner bred with Cornell University, is a semi-bush butternut-type winter squash sized for small gardens and containers.

directions: Direct sow into warm, fertile soil in full sun, or grow in a large container with support for the vines. Winter Honeybaby stays compact with semi-bush vines only 2-3 feet long, yet is remarkably productive, bearing numerous personal-size, light-bulb-shaped fruits with sweet, nutty orange flesh meatier than comparable mini squash. The variety shows good powdery mildew tolerance and resists cracking, making it reliable through a long storage-squash season. Allow fruit to fully mature and cure in the sun for a few days before storing for winter use.

common_name: Magellan Coral Zinnia (AAS-Winning Compact Dahlia-Flowered Zinnia)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil is warm, or start indoors 4-6 weeks earlier for an earlier bloom; Magellan Coral, a 2005 All-America Selections winner bred by Goldsmith Seeds, reaches first bloom in just 6-9 weeks from sowing.

directions: Sow seed directly into full sun once the soil has warmed, or start indoors for a head start on bloom. Magellan Coral produces fully double, 5-6 inch dahlia-type flowers in a brilliant coral shade on a compact, uniform plant that stays shorter and tidier than older tall dahlia-flowered zinnias. It needs no deadheading or staking, tolerates heat well, and makes an excellent cut flower as well as a pollinator draw. Even, consistent watering through the heat of summer keeps the large blooms coming without interruption.

common_name: Prestige Scarlet Celosia (AAS-Winning Deep Red Crested Cockscomb)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant only after all danger of frost has passed; Prestige Scarlet, a 1997 All-America Selections winner bred by Sakata Seed, is a heat-tolerant crested cockscomb type.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights are reliably warm, since this heat-loving variety stalls in cool soil. Prestige Scarlet produces velvety, deep scarlet cockscomb-type combs up to 3.5 inches wide that cover the entire plant for a prolonged summer-to-frost bloom period on a vigorous, easy-to-grow, upright habit. It needs no staking and tolerates heat and humidity with carefree performance, making it dependable for bedding displays. The long-lasting combs also dry and cut well for fresh or dried arrangements.

common_name: Black Olive Ornamental Pepper (AAS-Winning Purple-Black Fruited Ornamental Pepper)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost under high light at 60-70 degrees F and transplant once frost danger has passed; Black Olive, a 2012 All-America Selections winner, is grown chiefly for its dark ornamental fruit and foliage rather than for eating.

directions: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost, then transplant into full sun in well-drained soil after frost danger has passed. Black Olive maintains an upright habit with dark purple-black foliage and small clustered fruit that emerges deep purple-black before maturing to red, set off by bright purple flowers for season-long ornamental contrast. It tolerates heat well, needs no deadheading or staking, and performs equally well as a border specimen, container plant, or cut-flower element. The fruit is technically edible and very hot but is grown primarily for its dramatic color display rather than culinary use.
